geometry.rationale: Figure 1 better reconstructs the apparatus as a continuous outlined glass bulb-and-U-tube with separate gas and liquid fills, a proper closed-end dome/open-end alternative, valve, pressure arrow, and height marker integrated at the correct relative liquid levels. Figure 2 captures the same manometer cases and equations, but its tube is approximated with thick centerline strokes rather than a true outlined vessel, the gas region is mostly missing from the connecting/vertical arm, the closed end appears as a gray plug rather than glass, and the reference/height lines are less faithful in styling and placement.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 1 has fewer requested controls, but its implemented controls are more internally consistent: changing the manometer type and pressure recomputes the liquid levels and displays a formula whose sign matches the drawn column positions. Figure 2 covers more of the requested interaction list, including three radio modes and better derivation popups, but its controls are less correct: selecting “gas below atm” or “gas above atm” changes the slider behind the user’s back, and then dragging the pressure slider across atmospheric pressure leaves the radio label contradicting the drawn geometry and formula; additionally the closed-end height is capped so high-pressure slider changes no longer produce proportional drawn h while the tooltip value continues to change.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is more visually faithful overall because it preserves more of the original closed-end manometer’s color scheme, shaded gas/mercury regions, labeled closed end/vacuum, and textbook-style formula placement. Figure 2 has a cleaner h marker and broadly similar geometry, but it is more simplified and less like the original in styling, with a much larger gas bulb, missing pale gas fill in the tubing, and a less faithful closed-end cap/line treatment.

labels.rationale: Figure 2 has clearer, larger, and better-placed diagram labels for Gas, Closed end, Vacuum, h, and the formula, with leader lines that do not crowd the artwork. Figure 1 includes the same essential closed-end labels, but they are smaller, the h annotation is more cramped within the tube gap, and the label/formula readability is weaker at inline size; both figures include extra interface text not in the original, but Figure 2’s core diagram labeling is closer and cleaner.

concept.rationale: Figure 1 keeps the liquid height difference proportional to the pressure difference for the closed-end and open-end cases and assigns the correct signs: closed-end vacuum gives P_gas = hρg, gas-side higher in an open manometer gives P_gas = P_atm − hρg, and open-arm higher gives P_gas = P_atm + hρg (L00010, L00014, L00017). Figure 2 also gets these sign relationships and equations mostly right, but its drawn height difference is capped for larger closed-end pressures, so increasing P_gas no longer visibly increases h in direct proportion even while the narration says it does, which weakens the core proportionality that h measures pressure (L00007, L00010, L00012, L00017).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is stronger overall because it more accurately reconstructs the manometer geometry and preserves the core pressure-height relationships across closed- and open-end cases, with controls that remain internally consistent. Figure 2 has clearer labels and more interaction coverage, but it is less reliable: its vessel rendering is more schematic, its pressure-mode controls can contradict the displayed geometry/formula, and its capped closed-end height breaks the proportional relationship that Figure 1 maintains.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 better preserves the textbook cross-section as a labeled Hall-Héroult cell: it shows the steel shell, ceramic lining, electrolyte, crust, molten aluminum layer, carbon cathode floor, two carbon anodes with yokes, positive and negative terminals, exhaust duct, and visibly clustered gas bubbles at the anodes. Figure 2 has cleaner nested tank proportions, but its static bubbles are effectively hidden behind lower layers at the initial state, leaving a labeled bubble region blank, and it adds moving ion labels not typical of the original structure while simplifying some terminal/hood geometry.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 2's play checkbox, current slider, and step controls consistently update the animation state, bubble/ion spawning rates, and aluminum thickness, including sensible behavior at 0 and high current. Figure 1's current slider does increase bubbles and aluminum thickness, but its Run electrolysis button is initialized backwards—clicking the advertised run button actually pauses because the internal running state starts true—and it does not animate Al³⁺ reduction or O²⁻ oxidation ions, only bubbles and layer growth.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is more visually faithful: it preserves the distinctive Hall-Héroult cell composition with two detailed carbon anodes, green electrolyte layer with bubble dots, gray molten aluminum band, black cathode, peach ceramic lining, dark steel shell, and similarly placed callout labels. Figure 2 is recognizable but much more simplified and proportionally different, with missing bubble texture, plainer anodes, cramped/overlapping left labels, and a layout that looks less like the original textbook figure at a glance.

labels.rationale: Figure 1 includes essentially all of the original diagram labels with clearer, larger text and better leader-line placement, while Figure 2’s labels are noticeably smaller and several are cramped or colliding with the vessel on the left, making 'Ceramic' and 'Steel shell' especially hard to read. Figure 2 also has more clutter from added explanatory sidebar text, whereas Figure 1’s diagram annotations more closely match the reference and remain more legible at inline size.

concept.rationale: Figure 1 is conceptually more accurate because it consistently shows and labels Al₂O₃ in molten Na₃AlF₆, positive carbon anodes, a negative carbon cathode floor, molten aluminum collected above the cathode, and O₂/CO/CO₂ bubbles at the anodes, matching the Hall-Héroult process described in the brief (L00012-L00014, L00019). Figure 2 gets the main layout largely right, but its anode popup says oxygen is oxidized to form CO and CO₂, which misstates the anode chemistry: oxide discharge and carbon-anode oxidation produce the gaseous products, and the required products include O₂ as well as CO and CO₂ (L00007, L00012, L00019).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is stronger overall because it more faithfully preserves the Hall-Héroult cell geometry, labels, and conceptual chemistry: it shows the layered vessel, anodes/cathode, electrolyte, molten aluminum, terminals, and gas bubbles in a form closer to the textbook reference, with clearer annotations. Figure 2 has better-functioning interactive controls and richer animation behavior, but compared with Figure 1 it is visually more simplified, has cramped/less legible labels, initially obscures the bubble region, and includes a chemistry popup that misstates the anode process.

geometry.rationale: Figure 2 better matches the likely textbook geometry by reconstructing both the 3D loss-surface panel and the separate 2D contour/heatmap panel, with appropriate parameter ranges, contour ellipses, markers, descent path, and labeled axes. Figure 1 has a reasonable convex 3D bowl and grid, but it replaces the separate contour subplot with a toggle/flattened view, uses a different optimum and marker layout, and its full bounding box/grid and surface scaling appear less faithful to the original spatial arrangement.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 2 has the more correct interaction set: the draggable current parameter marker updates both the 3D surface and the inset heatmap, the loss readout follows it, the gradient-descent button recomputes steps from the current position, and the learning-rate slider affects subsequent descent behavior including slow, fast, and overshooting cases. Figure 1’s controls mostly work, but it substitutes a 3D/2D toggle for simultaneous synchronized panels, so the advertised heatmap synchronization is much weaker, and its gradient descent is clamped to the parameter bounds, which can mask the true large-learning-rate behavior. Figure 2 is not perfect because high learning rates can push the marker/path outside the plotted domain and a divergent step can leave the 3D marker stale relative to the stored parameters, but overall its interactions match the intended synchronized surface/heatmap descent behavior better than Figure 1.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 2 is more recognizable as the textbook figure because it includes both the 3D loss surface and the 2D contour view with similar brown loss coloring, elliptical contours, labels, and point markers. Figure 1 only shows the 3D surface in the screenshot and its view is more distorted and dark, with extra contour rings on the surface and UI dominating the composition, making it less immediately resemble the original multipanel figure.

labels.rationale: Figure 2 has more of the required textbook annotations, including axis labels for the 3D plot and the contour plot, plus an 'a)' panel marker, whereas Figure 1 only shows the 3D view and omits the corresponding contour-panel labels entirely. Figure 2 is still cluttered and has some invented/overlapping annotations such as the orange loss label and UI text, but Figure 1's labels are very small, missing important panel labeling, and include extra unrelated interface/demo text and point annotations that do not match the original.

concept.rationale: Figure 2 more accurately teaches the requested relationship between the 3D loss landscape and the corresponding top-down contour/heatmap by showing a labeled a) surface together with a labeled b) inset heatmap, with the same example markers and an explicit optimum visible in both; Figure 1 instead substitutes a single toggleable view for the two panels and lacks true panel labels, so the correspondence is less faithfully asserted (L00007). Figure 1 does better on the stated 0–70 loss scaling, while Figure 2's loss axis effectively tops out around 60 rather than 70, but both still use a smooth convex quadratic surface with no spurious local minima, and Figure 2 better conveys the main two-view supervised-loss concept overall (L00007).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 2 is stronger overall because it reconstructs the intended paired presentation: a 3D loss surface together with a synchronized 2D contour/heatmap, with clearer textbook-style axis labels, panel labeling, markers, descent path, and parameter/loss interactions. Figure 1 has a plausible convex surface and working controls, but it substitutes a toggleable single view for the simultaneous two-panel comparison, omits important contour-panel labeling, and is less faithful visually due to its darker/distorted rendering, extra UI emphasis, and less accurate spatial/layout arrangement.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 is geometrically closer: it models the image as a square 3D slab with raised grid strips, correct regular and half-offset window partitions including partial edge windows, and includes the full a)–f) sequence with original, 4×4, shifted 4×4, 2×2, shifted 2×2, and 1×1 states. interactivity.rationale: Figure 1 has some real edge-case faults—the window slider incorrectly allows an unsupported 3×3 state, and offset mode at N=1 can create a nonsensical split instead of the degenerate single window—but its handlers generally rebuild the current grid, keep the UI synchronized, include all demo states, and tile clicks operate on the current tile list. Figure 2 maps the slider values more cleanly to 1/2/4 divisions, but its click interaction is likely to become incorrect after any rebuild because it registers new interactive tile meshes without unregistering the old removed ones, so raycasts can select stale tiles from previous regular/offset/grid states; it also omits demo states like the original image and 2×2 offset and only draws a star from one token rather than clearly highlighting all within-window attention.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is more visually faithful because it preserves the grey graffiti-wall look, the cartoon figure, dark 4×4 window grid, slab-like perspective, and captioning that match the reference’s window-partition panels. Figure 2 shows the same general idea but is much paler and more abstract, with oversized white dividers, simplified/cropped artwork, and a washed-out colour scheme that makes it less immediately recognizable as the original textbook figure.

labels.rationale: Figure 1 includes the original-style demo labels in the interface and shows the active caption “b) 4×4 windows,” whereas Figure 2 lacks the a)–f) panel labels and the original captions under the visual entirely, replacing them with explanatory UI text. Figure 1’s visible bottom caption is somewhat cramped and overlaps the artwork edge, but it still matches the textbook labeling much better than Figure 2’s missing/invented annotations.

concept.rationale: Figure 1 more accurately teaches the specified Swin shifted-window partitioning scheme: it provides the original-image state plus regular and half-window-offset variants for 4×4 and 2×2 partitions and the 1×1 case, with captions matching the requested a)–f) sequence and an explanation that alternating regular and offset windows permits cross-boundary information flow without global-attention cost (L00007). aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is the clear overall winner because it more faithfully matches the intended Swin shifted-window figure: it includes the full a)–f) sequence, the original-image state, regular and shifted 4×4 and 2×2 partitions, the 1×1 case, closer slab-like geometry, and more faithful labels and visual styling. Figure 2 captures the broad idea of window partitioning but is weaker by omitting key demo states such as the original panel and shifted 2×2 case, using a flatter and less faithful rendering with missing textbook labels, and having less reliable interaction due to stale selectable tiles after rebuilds.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 better reconstructs the likely textbook geometry: it has a wireframe joint-distribution box with multiple parallel slice planes through the latent direction, density patterns on those planes, a curved manifold passing through the slices, a separate marginal panel with matching orientation, and a connecting marginalization arrow. Figure 2 captures the general idea but introduces extra geometry not in the source, such as a posterior strip, drag marker, and multiple UI-driven demo elements, and its marginal panel is oddly rotated in 3D rather than placed as a clean adjacent projection panel; its slice construction also appears less faithful, using separate blob planes rather than full colored slice distributions.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 2 implements functioning controls for all three intended interactions: the z slider moves and redraws the slice, the marginalization button animates a sweep while updating the marginal texture, and the draggable observation point recomputes a posterior-like red profile along the z axis. Figure 1's only substantive control is the z slider, which appears to update its slice correctly, but it lacks any working marginalization animation or draggable posterior interaction, so it is much less complete on interaction correctness.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is more recognizable as the reference because it preserves the main composition of a wireframe 3D volume with multiple dark probability slices, glowing density spots, a cyan curved trajectory with points/arrow, and a separate marginal heatmap panel with similar labeling and the grey marginalization arrow. Figure 2 captures some elements, but the cube is simplified to only a couple of slices, the cyan path through the 3D volume is largely replaced by a vertical arrow and an extra red curve, and the marginal panel is small and positioned under the cube rather than as the prominent separate panel, making the overall resemblance weaker.

labels.rationale: Figure 1 has fewer extraneous labels and its core labels x1, x2, z, Pr(x,z|φ), Pr(x|φ), and the marginalization text are mostly present and readable, whereas Figure 2 adds many non-original UI button and instruction labels that clutter the screenshot. Figure 2 does include x1 and x2 labels on the marginal panel that Figure 1 lacks, but its annotation area is more crowded and the marginalization text overlaps the main diagram more noticeably.

concept.rationale: Figure 2 more accurately maps the latent coordinate z to slice planes and shows the nonlinear decoder manifold x=f(z) with conditional probability blobs on those slices, then accumulates those blobs into a 2D marginal panel, so the core relationship between Pr(x,z|φ) and Pr(x|φ) is clearer and truer to the brief (L00007). Figure 1 also conveys marginalization, but it relies more on a single cyan curve plus a few heatmap planes rather than a family of z-conditioned projected curves, making the conditional-slice-to-marginal relationship less explicit (L00007). Both figures miss the requested multi-colored family of curves, and Figure 2 adds an unsupported posterior interaction whose computation is not the stated figure concept, but its main VAE latent-manifold and marginalization depiction is still conceptually stronger than Figure 1's.

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is stronger overall because it more faithfully reconstructs the reference geometry and rendered composition: a wireframe joint-distribution volume with multiple probability slices, a cyan manifold, a separate marginal heatmap panel, and a clear marginalization arrow, while Figure 2 simplifies and rearranges these elements and adds unsupported demo/posterior geometry. Figure 2 is clearly better for implemented interactions and has some conceptual clarity in its z-slice accumulation, but its extra UI labels, posterior strip/marker, smaller displaced marginal panel, and weaker visual resemblance make it less faithful to the intended figure than Figure 1.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 reconstructs the perspective-projection geometry much more completely: it has a correctly placed pinhole O, an image plane between O and the receding bird path, multiple equally spaced 3D bird positions, projection rays through the plane, shrinking projected silhouettes/dots, image-plane velocity arrows, and a vanishing point computed from the flight direction. Figure 2 captures the basic idea but is geometrically sparser and less faithful: it uses fewer bird positions, a simplified wire-outline bird, lacks the dashed flight path and projected dots, has less convincing proportions/element counts, and its projection/arrow construction is less visually aligned with the expected textbook diagram.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 1 implements the requested controls much more correctly: its looped animation, pause/scrub slider, demo-step tweening, direction drag, vanishing point, projected path, rays, image-plane arrows, and inset are all recomputed from the current bird position and direction, including sensible handling at the t=1 endpoint. Figure 2's time slider does update the scene, but it has no looped animation at all, no play/pause, and its direction drag is only a partial re-aim that changes V.x and V.y while keeping V.z fixed; it also lacks the lower image-plane interaction/view requested and has weaker degenerate handling in the drag-plane intersection.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is much more recognizable as the reference because it includes the receding sequence of bird silhouettes, red motion arrows, green projection/trajectory lines, an image plane with vanishing point labeling, and an inset image-plane view; Figure 2 reduces the scene to a tiny plane with a few faint lines and lacks the prominent birds, arrows, labels, and overall composition that define the original.

labels.rationale: Figure 1 includes several of the original annotations such as v, O, image plane, and vanishing point, though many are very small and some are cluttered or embedded in an extra inset/UI. Figure 2 has almost none of the required textbook labels visible or readable, aside from an unrelated UI control label, so it matches the original annotations much worse.

concept.rationale: Figure 1 more accurately teaches the full concept: it explicitly models a pinhole camera with O, an image plane between O and the receding bird positions, green projection rays, equal-length 3D V arrows, projected bird positions that shrink and converge to the labeled vanishing point, and image-plane arrows that shorten toward that same point, matching the required constant 3D velocity versus decreasing image velocity relationship (L00007-L00013, L00016). Figure 2 is broadly physically consistent in its projection and vanishing-point formula, but it is less conceptually complete and less direct: the image-plane view is mixed into the 3D plane rather than shown as the lower image-plane collapse, and the V labeling/sequence communicates the equal 3D velocity and shrinking projected velocity less clearly than Figure 1 (L00013, L00016).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is consistently stronger: it reconstructs the pinhole geometry with O, image plane, receding bird positions, projection rays, shrinking image-plane positions, velocity arrows, vanishing point, labels, and an inset view, while Figure 2 is much sparser and omits or weakens many of these textbook elements. Figure 1 also implements the intended interactions more completely with animation, pause/scrub behavior, direction dragging, and recomputed rays/vanishing point, whereas Figure 2 has only partial slider-based updates and weaker direction control.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 better reconstructs the intended pinhole-camera geometry: it places the sensor at z=-f, virtual image plane at z=+f, object panel at positive depth, uses correct mirrored sensor projection, includes the pixel grid with N/M proportions, principal point, projected dots, f bracket, local plane axes, and an inverted colored image patch. Figure 2 uses a much different house-shaped 3D object and larger coordinate scale, changes the sensor aspect/proportions, omits or simplifies several source relationships such as the principal point and neighbor/snapped pixel structure, and its initial viewpoint is less consistent with the sensor-left/object-right textbook layout.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 2's implemented controls generally do what they advertise: dragging P updates the ray, projections, active pixel and readouts; the sliders update geometry, grid resolution, labels, and sampled sensor image; and the demo step buttons correctly change state. Figure 1 covers more of the requested intrinsic-matrix readout, but its demo step handler is effectively broken because it assigns the tween function before checking `if (!tween)`, so the requested step changes never run; its sensor-centered readout is also not actually centered but offset by half the sensor, and off-sensor projections are clamped to an edge pixel rather than cleanly treated as out of bounds.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is more visually faithful because it preserves the textbook diagram’s core composition: a gridded image/sensor plane on the left, a camera center with projection rays, a virtual image plane, coordinate axes, and colored projected patches. Figure 2 includes some related elements, but the dominant red-roof/green house-like solid is an invented object that reads very differently from the original abstract colored planes, and its overall layout is less recognizable as the same figure.

labels.rationale: Figure 1 includes many of the original diagram labels and annotations, such as Image plane/sensor, N pixels, M pixels, Camera center, Virtual image plane, Optical/principal axis, f, and coordinate axes, even though they are somewhat small. Figure 2 largely lacks the textbook-style annotations on the diagram itself and instead shows mostly interface/control text, so important original labels are missing or not readable in the figure area.

concept.rationale: Figure 2 more consistently teaches the projection chain by separating the virtual-plane projection at +f from the inverted physical sensor hit at −f and then discretizing that hit into pixel indices, matching the requested camera-to-sensor sampling chain (L00007-L00012, L00015). Figure 1 includes more explicit K/pixel-size information, but it computes the displayed sensor/pixel location from the inverted physical sensor coordinate while displaying a positive-focal-scale K that would not map P to those same pixel indices, so its labels/readout assert an inconsistent intrinsic relationship (L00015). Figure 2 is less complete about explicitly assembling K and uses a fixed scene depth in its implementation, but it makes fewer false geometric assertions than Figure 1.

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is the stronger overall match because it more faithfully reconstructs the intended pinhole-camera diagram, with the sensor/image plane, virtual image plane, camera center, projection rays, pixel grid proportions, principal axis, focal-length bracket, and original-style labels that Figure 2 largely omits or replaces with UI text. Figure 2 has better functioning controls and a somewhat cleaner projection-chain interaction, but compared with Figure 1 it introduces an invented house-like object, changes the layout and proportions, and drops important textbook annotations and geometric relationships. Figure 1 does have interaction/readout inconsistencies, yet its high-confidence advantages in geometry, visual faithfulness, and labeling outweigh Figure 2’s moderate advantages in interactivity and conceptual implementation.

geometry.rationale: Figure 2 reconstructs the 3D camera-geometry diagram more faithfully: the image plane, observed points, reprojected points, world points, residual segments, and dashed projection rays are arranged with clearer collinearity and correct in-plane residual geometry, and it includes the K/R/T perturbations implied by reprojection error. Figure 1 captures the broad idea with a plane, three 3D points, projected points, and error vectors, but its geometry is more schematic and arbitrary: the plane placement/proportions and point layout are less source-specific, the camera error is reduced mostly to focal length and x-translation, and the projection rays/residual construction are less complete.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 2 is better because its K/R/T sliders all recompute the reprojected points, residual segments, labels, rays, and SSE, and it implements dragging for both observed and reprojected image points, whereas Figure 1 only has focal length and X-translation sliders and no drag support at all. Figure 1's aggregate-error toggle is also substantially flawed because the SSE HTML label is managed as a normal scene label and will be re-shown by the label sync even in per-point mode, and it never displays numeric individual residuals. Figure 2 is not perfect: hiding individual residual labels in total mode is similarly undermined by the label sync, and dragging a reprojected point manually updates only that residual rather than the underlying estimated model or total SSE panel, but it still covers and recomputes far more of the intended interactions correctly than Figure 1.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 2 is more recognizable as the reference because it preserves the main composition of a large orange 3D triangle to the right of a vertical image plane, with a smaller projected orange triangle on the plane, dashed correspondence lines, colored vertices, labels, axes, and red residual vectors. Figure 1 contains many of the same elements, but the geometry is more compressed and rearranged, with the large triangle appearing on the wrong side/at an odd scale relative to the image plane, making the overall resemblance to the textbook figure weaker at a glance.

labels.rationale: Figure 2 has noticeably more readable and better placed diagram labels, including visible P1/P2/P3 and XL/YL/ZL axis labels, whereas Figure 1’s diagram labels are extremely small and mostly illegible at inline size. concept.rationale: Figure 2 represents the core definition more completely: the same three 3D points P_i form a scene triangle, project to observed p_i, and are reprojected to p′_i using estimated K, R, and T parameters, with red residuals lying on the image plane and an explicit sum-of-squares objective consistent with the text (L00017-L00023, L00025, L00028). Figure 1 is mostly conceptually correct, but its estimated model only varies focal length and x translation and its objective display is less explicitly tied to the 2D residual definition; Figure 2 therefore teaches the intended relationship between estimated camera parameters and reprojection error more accurately, despite its extra draggable p′ interaction being a slight conceptual risk because p′ should be computed from the estimated model rather than freely placed (L00020-L00022, L00028).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 2 is the clear overall winner: compared with Figure 1, it more faithfully preserves the reference composition, has more legible labels, and reconstructs the camera-geometry relationship with clearer image-plane residuals, projection rays, world points, and K/R/T perturbations. It also implements substantially more of the intended interactivity, with sliders and dragging that update more of the diagram, whereas Figure 1 is more schematic, less readable, offers only focal-length and x-translation controls, lacks dragging, and has weaker handling of error displays. Figure 2 still has minor interaction and conceptual issues around label syncing and freely dragging reprojected points, but these are outweighed by its stronger geometry, labeling, visual faithfulness, and coverage of the intended concept.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 better matches the likely textbook structure: it uses a clean coordinate layout with two orange squares, prominent black axes, a single solid red translation arrow with arrowhead and label, and proportions that keep the translated square and vector as the focus. Figure 2 adds extra gridlines and a large matrix overlay inside the plotting area, uses different axis proportions and thinner styling, and places the translated square farther away, making the reconstruction less faithful to the simple 2D translation diagram.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 1 recomputes and redraws the square positions, arrows, and both the single and composed homogeneous matrices for sliders, drag handles, moved-square dragging, and chain-mode toggling, so it covers the intended interactions more completely. Figure 2's square dragging and chained toggle do update the geometry and matrix, but it lacks direct tx/ty or second-translation controls beyond dragging, and its drag interaction snaps/clamps values to coarse bounded half-unit positions, making it less complete and less faithful to freely setting the translation vectors.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is more visually faithful because it preserves the textbook figure’s bold black axes, large orange squares with black outlines, red translation arrow, and italic labels in a similar composition. labels.rationale: Figure 1 has the essential diagram labels x, y, and t in large, readable italic text placed similarly to the textbook figure, while Figure 2's x, y, and t labels are much smaller and less comfortable to read at inline size. Figure 2 also adds a prominent matrix annotation in the drawing area that is not part of the original, creating extra clutter; Figure 1 has some extra UI text on the side, but its main figure labels are clearer and better placed.

concept.rationale: Both figures correctly show a translation as adding vector t to the square’s position and preserve the square’s size/orientation, matching x'=x+t_x and y'=y+t_y (L00007-L00024, L00053-L00054), and both show that applying t then s reaches the same final position as t+s (L00026, L00053-L00054). Figure 1 is conceptually stronger because it explicitly annotates the coordinate update and the homogeneous translation matrix, and in chained mode states the correct column-vector composition T(s)·T(t)=T(t+s), directly aligning the vector-sum and matrix-composition ideas (L00028-L00030, L00053-L00054). Figure 2 is also largely correct, but its chained matrix display is less explicit about multiplication between T(s) and T(t), so it teaches the same relationship a bit less precisely than Figure 1.

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is stronger across all dimensions: it more faithfully preserves the textbook-style composition with bold axes, large orange squares, a clear red translation vector, and readable x/y/t labels, while Figure 2’s grid, thin axes, smaller marks, and prominent matrix overlay make it feel less like the intended diagram. It also provides more complete and precise interactive/conceptual support, including freer translation controls, chained translations, and explicit homogeneous matrix composition, whereas Figure 2 is more limited and less explicit despite representing the basic translation idea correctly.
